rashi:a2.1: A majority that depends on an action: such as an animal’s pregnancy, which depends on mating, and one must be concerned that perhaps no male mounted it. Therefore it is uncertain.
rashi:a5.1: But I myself do not say so: I do not disagree with you in the words of the tradition I received, but in other words [of my own]. Below [the Gemara] explains what difference there is between his reasoning and his tradition.
rashi:a6.1: In what do Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree: [that is, Rabbi Yishmael and] Rabbi Yehoshua’s tradition, which he taught as “but they said.”
rashi:a6.2: They disagree whether a murky discharge exempts: Rabbi Yishmael, who treats it as a definite firstborn, holds that even if it did expel a discharge within its first year, it is not exempted.
rashi:a8.1: To a stringency: as at the start of this passage [on 19b], where, had we followed the majority, we would treat [the offspring of an animal] from that point forward as definitely exempt. So he is concerned for the minority as a stringency and treats it as uncertain. But here, being concerned for the minority would be a leniency, since even [the offspring of] one within its first year would be treated as uncertain.
rashi:a10.1: His tradition: “but they said” (it accepts Ze’eiri’s statement).
rashi:a10.2: His reasoning: “And I myself do not say so,” etc.
rashi:a11.1: That expelled a murky discharge at the end of six: we saw that it began to expel the discharge at the beginning of the seventh month.
rashi:a11.2: There is no murky discharge of less than thirty days: it does not accept a male for thirty days.
rashi:a12.1: According to his tradition: where we do not know that it expelled a discharge at six months, he disagrees with Rabbi Yishmael, who said that [the offspring of one] within its first year is definitely the priest’s; he tells him that even if it gave birth within its first year it is uncertain, since perhaps it expelled a discharge three or four months after it was born and then gave birth again within its year. And where we saw that it did not expel a discharge until the end of six months, and it expelled one at the end of six, as Rabbi Yehoshua said in his reasoning, that is a full firstborn, since that discharge was not a full discharge. Had it been a discharge, it would not give birth within its year but only on the first day of the second year: the discharge takes the whole seventh month, as Ze’eiri says, and the five months of pregnancy [follow], so its year is over, and it gives birth only on the next day, since all the months of pregnancy must be complete and only then does it give birth, on the next day. As we say in Tractate Nidda (38b): “And the Lord gave her conception [herayon]” (Ruth 4:13): herayon has the numerical value 271; nine months of thirty days make 270 days, and on day 271 the verse writes that she gives birth.
rashi:a12.2: According to his reasoning: even though we saw that it did not expel a discharge until the end of six, it is still uncertain, since he does not accept Ze’eiri’s statement.
tosafot:a1.1: It is clear that Rabbi Yishmael holds like Rabbi Meir, who is concerned for the minority: and for the reason of “combine the minority”: combine the minority [of animals] that do not conceive with the presumption that it has not given birth, and the majority is weakened, so it cannot be counted a definite firstborn, since it is only half and half, as said at the beginning of the last chapter of Yevamot (119a), where I discussed it at length. And as for ruling pure in a case of uncertain impurity in the chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 86a), that is because we derive from the sota that [an uncertainty about] something without the awareness to be asked is pure. That is why it says there: if they said an uncertain impurity is pure, shall they say an uncertain prohibition is permitted?
tosafot:a2.1: Ravina said: You may even say the Rabbis: this is puzzling: why does [the Gemara] not answer this way at the beginning of the last chapter of Yevamot (119a), on the mishna that she may not marry or enter levirate marriage until she knows whether her rival wife is pregnant? One may answer that human intercourse is not regarded as dependent on an action the way animal mating is, since an animal sometimes has to be brought to mate, as said in the chapter HaSokher et HaPoalim (Bava Metzia 91a): one may insert it like a kohl stick into a tube.
tosafot:a7.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds one is concerned about a murky discharge: And if you say: we conclude below that Rabbi Yehoshua is not concerned for a minority, as is inferred from the mishna “If she left full… Rabbi Yehoshua says she need not be concerned”; so how is he concerned here for the minority [of animals] that expel a discharge? Furthermore, in a case like this even Rabbi Meir is not concerned, as said at the beginning of the last chapter of Yevamot (119b): where there is a majority and a presumption, the minority is a minority of a minority; and here there is a majority that do not expel a discharge and the presumption that it has not given birth. One may answer that in any case it is not a definite firstborn to be given to the priest, since there is the presumption of [the owner’s] money, which is stronger, and the burden of proof rests on the one who takes from another. Even according to Rav, who follows the majority in monetary matters in the case of one who sells an ox that is found to be a gorer (Bava Kamma 46a), that is because [the buyer] says: I am sure of myself that I am of the majority. Alternatively, one may distinguish between money that has no claimants and money that has claimants. Yet it is somewhat puzzling that for flogging over shearing and labor, and for being offered on the altar, it counts as a definite firstborn because we follow the majority and the presumption, while for giving it to the priest it would count as uncertain. It seems one should answer that we are concerned here for the minority that expel a discharge because most animals conceive once they reach the age at which they are fit to conceive.
tosafot:a8.1: When it leads to a leniency he is not concerned: and it is even given to the priest, since it is offered on the altar. Yet with a donkey this is difficult: we should leave the money with the owners and not follow the majority, since even Rav agrees here that in monetary matters we do not follow the majority, as I explained above. One may answer that the donkey was decreed on account of a kosher animal.
tosafot:a9.1: In brief: And if you wish, say: whether to a leniency or a stringency he is concerned. Earlier too, when [the Gemara] wanted to say he is not concerned to a leniency, that implies it is only Rabbi Yishmael’s view, and Rabbi Meir is concerned everywhere. Still, one cannot infer from here that Rabbi Meir’s concern for the minority is by Torah law because he is concerned here even to be lenient, i.e., not to give it to the priest: in monetary matters we do not follow the majority; alternatively, the majority [of animals] that conceive once they reach the fitting age supports the minority. In the chapter Ein Ma’amidin (Avoda Zara 34b), on the cheese of Beit Unyaki, it says Rabbi Meir is concerned for the minority and decreed on the majority because of the minority, but did not decree on other places because of that place; this implies that even in that place it is rabbinic, a decree because of the minority. Likewise the first chapter of Ḥullin (12a) asks, for Rabbi Meir: what can be said of the Paschal offering and sacrifices, which the Merciful One permitted?, and does not ask about ordinary meat. This implies the concern is rabbinic: even if they decreed on ordinary meat, they did not decree on the Paschal offering and sacrifices, where [checking] is impossible, and where they could not uphold their decree they upheld it where possible. So too by Torah law, possible and impossible are treated alike; were they not, the Sages would not have decreed where checking is possible once they saw a case, such as the impossible one, where there is no concern. But where a presumption supports the minority, it seems Rabbi Meir is concerned by Torah law, since he rules pure in the case of the child [who handles the dough], and in the chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 86b) he wishes to permit slaughtering “it and its offspring” after a slaughter by a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor, although most of their acts are not ruined. And if you say: the chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 55b), on the five fifths, implies demai is rabbinic even for Rabbi Meir, since it says “they reinforced their words”; why is it not tevel by Torah law, combining the minority who do not tithe with the presumption of tevel? One may answer that this is no presumption, since perhaps [the owner] did as Rabbi Oshaya taught and brought it in with its chaff (Berakhot 31a); and further, one does not presume any person wicked because of the minority who do not tithe. gershom:a1.1: Rather, it is clear, etc. [The Rabbis follow the majority] with a majority that does not depend on an action, such as a eunuch and a sexually underdeveloped woman [ailonit], who are so of themselves.
gershom:a2.1: But with a majority that depends on an action: in that case they do not follow the majority but are concerned for the minority. What is the action? Whether a male mounted it or not.
gershom:a3.1: Like a cow: that within its third year it is definitely the priest’s.
gershom:a4.1: Until here are the words of Rabbi Yishmael: that is, it is as the words of Rabbi Yishmael [in the mishna].
gershom:a5.1: A goat that expelled a murky discharge at six months gives birth within its year: since the discharge is in the seventh month, it conceives at the end of the seventh, carries five months and gives birth at the end of its year; and the discharge exempts from the firstborn.
gershom:a6.1: I have not arrived at this measure: since I do not know whether it expels a discharge at the end of six or not.
gershom:a7.1: Rather, whatever is known, etc. And if uncertain: Rabbi Akiva is stringent, treating it as uncertain in every case, even within its first year.
gershom:a8.1: Rabbi Yishmael holds a murky discharge does not exempt: that is why he says it is definitely the priest’s, since it has not yet given birth; and even if it expelled a discharge earlier, it was not exempted by that.
gershom:a9.1: Rabbi Yishmael holds [we are not concerned about a murky discharge]: since we did not see it, we are not concerned about a discharge, given that it gave birth within its year, since it does not do both.
gershom:a10.1: But doesn’t Rava say: It is clear that [Rabbi Yishmael] holds like Rabbi Meir, who is concerned for the minority, even where it is not before us and we did not see it; here too let him be concerned about a discharge, though we did not see it.
gershom:a11.1: When he is concerned, it is to a stringency: to make it liable to the firstborn, since a minority of animals do not give birth within their year; and of this one too, say it did not give birth, and it is liable to the firstborn. But here, being concerned for the minority that expel a discharge would be a leniency, and it would be exempt from the firstborn.
gershom:a12.1: And I myself do not say so: [the Gemara] is explaining the baraita, as in “the Master said.”
gershom:a13.1: What is the difference between his tradition and his reasoning: “but they said” is his tradition, what he learned from his teacher; his reasoning is “and I myself do not say so.” And by the words of both it implies that a discharge exempts.
gershom:a14.1: For example, where it expelled a discharge at the end of six months from its birth, when the seventh month begins.
gershom:a15.1: And the difference between them is Ze’eiri’s [statement], who said: a discharge takes thirty days.
gershom:a16.1: According to his tradition: which does not state “gives birth within its year,” implying that it gives birth on the first day at the beginning of the second year.
gershom:a17.1: He accepts Ze’eiri’s [statement]: that it expels a discharge for thirty full days and is pregnant for five full months, which is the pregnancy of a small animal; so it turns out that it gives birth one day into the second year.
rashi:b1.1: According to his tradition we do not say an animal gives birth after incomplete months: therefore it did not mention the end of six.
rashi:b1.2: According to his reasoning we say so: since he does not derive an animal from a woman. Part of the last day of the fifth month of pregnancy counts as all of it, and it gives birth on that very day. Therefore, even if we accept Ze’eiri’s statement, and it conceived in Marḥeshvan, it gives birth on the last day of Adar, which is [still] its year.
rashi:b2.1: Part of the day: [the day] on which the fifth month, or the month of the discharge, is completed.
rashi:b2.2: This is the reading: “According to his tradition, we do not say part of the day is like all of it.”
rashi:b3.1: What difference is there between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua: for in less time than this, can it give birth? [Both seem to treat the same cases as uncertain.]
rashi:b4.1: Milk exempts: if it gives milk even within its first year; or if it was born in a Jew’s home and we did not see it give birth until after its first year, and it gives milk.
rashi:b4.2: Rabbi Yehoshua holds: a murky discharge exempts, but not milk.
rashi:b5.1: If she had a mother-in-law: a woman who went overseas with her husband, and her husband died without children and has no brother, and she has a mother-in-law in the place she left.
rashi:b5.2: She need not be concerned: that perhaps a son was born to her father-in-law and she is bound to a yavam.
rashi:b5.3: If she left full: if her mother-in-law was pregnant when this woman left there, she must be concerned.
rashi:b6.1: And half females: who do not bind her to levirate marriage.
rashi:b7.1: Rather, reverse: the answer is that Rabbi Yehoshua holds a murky discharge exempts, and the same applies to milk; and Rabbi Akiva comes to say: whatever is known to have given birth for the first time, even by a discharge, the priest has nothing here, etc.; if uncertain, [it is uncertain] even if it gives milk.
rashi:b7.2: And it is taught: said as support, not as a challenge.
rashi:b8.1: A kid: it mentions this because it is the way of goats to bear many young in one pregnancy.
rashi:b8.2: I saw a kid that was tithed within its year: that is, within the same year in which it bore the three daughters, the daughters in turn gave birth, so that all of them, they and their daughters, entered the pen to be tithed that year. Below [the Gemara] asks what difference this makes compared with the first tanna.
rashi:b8.3: A kid, three daughters: in one litter, and all her daughters gave birth three each. That is why it states “three” in the feminine: had they been males, they would not be tithed, since there would be three firstborns and then ten would not remain.
rashi:b8.4: All of them enter the pen to be tithed: together, since all of them, the three daughters and their nine daughters, can be born from Elul to Elul. Had they not been born in one year, they would not be tithed together, since the first of Elul is the new year for the animal tithe, and those born after Elul do not combine [with those born before], as explained in the chapter Ma’aser Behema (below, Bekhorot 57b). And these can be her daughters [and granddaughters] in one year, for example if the daughters were born on the first of Elul, conceived at the end of six months and gave birth before Elul. And why do I need to teach three daughters, all of whom gave birth, the three daughters, etc.
rashi:b8.5: [This explains the Gemara’s next question, on 21a.] Shall we say he holds that an animal that expels a murky discharge does not return and give birth within its year: [that is,] from the time of the discharge until the end of the year; and this one too cannot give birth [again], since it gave birth to three daughters at the beginning of the year. It mentions an animal that expels a discharge because one might have thought that one that expels a discharge also waits before giving birth, like one that gave birth; and [the Gemara] wishes to resolve from this as well whether the unattributed baraita follows the first tanna or Rabbi Yehoshua, who disagreed above about an animal that expels a discharge.
rashi:b8.6: [On 21a.] And it answers: even if you say that an animal that expels a discharge returns and gives birth [within its year], one that actually gave birth certainly does not return; that is everyone’s view.
rashi:b8.7: [This explains the Gemara’s answer on 21a.] There is a difference between them regarding Ze’eiri: for example, where the daughters expelled a discharge at the end of six months from their birth, at the beginning of the seventh month. The first tanna, who did not use the wording “within,” accepts Ze’eiri’s statement, that they do not accept a male again until the beginning of the eighth month, and their days of pregnancy are five full months, so it turns out that they give birth only on the first day of the second year. Even so, mothers and daughters can enter the pen together, all but the grandmother, for example in a leap year, when the first day of their second year is still the first of Av. And Rabbi Shimon, who used the wording “within its year,” [holds that] they were born on the last day of the year and lack time [before they may be offered] for seven days, and Rabbi Shimon holds that [even] those lacking time are tithed.
tosafot:b4.1: In brief: There is a difference between them whether milk exempts. Rabbeinu Tam ruled that milk does not exempt, since later in this chapter (24a) we conclude like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says that one who buys a nursing animal from a gentile is exempt from the firstborn because an animal shows no compassion [to nurse] unless it has given birth; milk alone does not exempt, only an offspring with it that we see it cherish and nurse. From this Rabbeinu Tam infers that the halakha is to be concerned for a minority where a presumption accompanies it, as here, where the animal is presumed not to have given birth; though we do not follow Rabbi Meir, who rules pure when “most children handle” (Nidda 18b) by combining the minority with the presumption, we are at least concerned to be stringent. And though the first chapter of Ḥullin (11b) implies the halakha is not like Rabbi Meir even to be stringent (“for Rabbi Meir, how does he eat meat?”, not “how do we eat meat?”), where a presumption supports [the minority] we are concerned. As for “most who are involved with slaughter are experts” (Ḥullin 3b), where we do not combine the minority who are not experts with the presumption of a forbidden animal: that majority is very common (as at the start of Gittin, 2b), and even Rabbi Meir is not concerned for an uncommon minority (Nidda 32a). So too with “waters without end” (Yevamot 121b), where after the fact the wife is permitted, the stringency at the outset being for the gravity of a married woman; with a goses, whom we do not presume dead to let his wife remarry; and in a place where most send gifts before betrothal, by Rabbeinu Ḥananel’s version in Kiddushin (50b). Question: why does the Gemara here challenge Rabbi Yehoshua, who says milk does not exempt, from his ruling “if she left full she need not be concerned” (Yevamot 119a) and resort to “reverse”? There no presumption accompanies the minority, while here the presumption accompanies the minority that give milk; and the mishna there proves the distinction, since in its first clause, explained there by combining a minority with a presumption, Rabbi Yehoshua does not dissent. Answer: since a baraita was found teaching the reverse, the Gemara did not trouble to answer otherwise. But after the reversal it is harder still: Rabbi Yehoshua says milk exempts, not concerned for the minority despite the presumption, while Yevamot implies he agrees in the first clause. Were we to say that here there is no presumption with the minority, since on the contrary the offspring is presumed not sanctified, being non-sacred in its mother’s womb, both points would be resolved; but then Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds milk does not exempt, would be concerned for a bare minority, whereas Kol HaTzelamim (Avoda Zara 40b) implies he is not. Further difficulties: Rabbi Yoḥanan follows Rabbi Meir on the cheeses of Beit Unyaki (Avoda Zara 39b), yet ate from a Kuti’s slaughter without concern for the suspect minority (Ḥullin 5b). Answers: many unattributed rulings ignore the minority, and there the unattributed ruling is followed by a dispute. Yet below (24a) Rabbi Yoḥanan rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the case of the pig wrapped around a ewe; answer: one does not presume all Kutim wicked, only that wicked one. And in Kiddushin (80a), on “most children handle,” Rabbi Yoḥanan seems to hold like the Rabbis; one may say he follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only because an animal shows no compassion unless it gave birth, the difference being where it had milk before giving birth. If so, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel may hold that milk exempts, and Rabbeinu Tam’s proof falls away. Still, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s rule that what lived thirty days is not a nefel, otherwise it is uncertain even if it fell from a roof or a lion ate it, shows concern for the minority of nefalim, against Kol HaTzelamim; and we rule both that we are not concerned for the minority (Ḥullin) and like him (Shabbat 136a). Answer: by law we would follow the Rabbis, and do so in time of need (Yevamot 37a); the Sages were stringent with the yevama lest people say it simply died and slander follow, and in mourning lest testimony be taken lightly, and in mourning the lenient view prevails anyway; and for an animal within eight days they followed him so that one would not slaughter it when sick and near death. Nor can one prove that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel ignores the minority from Makkot (7a), where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon ask whether the victim had a hole at the place of the sword and he says they would multiply murderers: that minority is treated as impossible to check, or no one would ever be executed, and even Rabbi Meir agrees (Ḥullin 11b). The Gemara could have challenged Rabbi Akiva from there but did not lengthen. Rabbeinu Tam rejects explaining Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon by concern for the minority at all, and the suggestion that the testimony is void once the witnesses say “we do not know” is also rejected; the case is not truly impossible to check, since the brain’s membrane could be exposed and seen whole, and Ḥullin calls it impossible only because the verse would otherwise be forced. gershom:b1.1: According to his reasoning, in which he said it gives birth within its year: he certainly does not accept Ze’eiri’s [statement], but holds that it expels a discharge for less than thirty [days], conceives before thirty are complete, and gives birth within its year.
gershom:b2.1: According to his reasoning: in which he says it gives birth within its year.
gershom:b3.1: We say it gives birth after incomplete months: before five months are complete, from day to day.
gershom:b4.1: According to his tradition: which did not say “within its year.”
gershom:b5.1: We do not say part of the day of the thirtieth day ending the discharge is like all of it, that is, that the days of the discharge are already complete and it can conceive that very day and give birth on the last day of its year; rather, we require thirty full days of discharge, from moment to moment, and it gives birth only at the beginning of the second year. And according to his reasoning we say part of the day is like all of it.
gershom:b6.1: What difference is there between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua: [according to Rabbi Yehoshua’s] tradition, for both of them it is uncertain where it is not known.
gershom:b7.1: There is a difference between them whether milk exempts: if it gives milk within its year. Rabbi Akiva said, “Whatever is known to have given birth for the first time”: by his words, since it gives milk it is exempt, for this counts as known, since it does not give milk unless it gave birth.
gershom:b8.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua, who is concerned about a discharge, that is, a minority, since a minority expel a discharge, is concerned too for the minority that give milk though they do not give birth, and it is liable to the firstborn.
gershom:b9.1: If she had a mother-in-law overseas: a woman whose husband and her rival wife went overseas need not be concerned that perhaps [the mother-in-law] bore a son and she is bound to him.
gershom:b10.1: But if she left full, that is, pregnant, she must be concerned. And Rabbi Yehoshua says she need not be concerned, and may marry.
gershom:b11.1: Rather, reverse: Rabbi Yehoshua said milk exempts, just as a discharge exempts.
gershom:b12.1: Rabbi Akiva says it does not exempt; rather, [only] whatever is known to have certainly given birth for the first time. And [now] Rabbi Yehoshua’s statement does not contradict Rabbi Yehoshua’s.
gershom:b13.1: And it is taught: a support.
gershom:b14.1: A kid that gave birth to three daughters: at once, at the end of its year.
gershom:b15.1: And all the daughters gave birth three each: on completing their year.
gershom:b16.1: All of them enter the pen together to be tithed, except the kid. That is why it teaches “all of them enter the pen,” since we say below that one does not tithe from last year’s [animals] on this year’s.
gershom:b17.1: I saw: a kid whose daughters were tithed.
gershom:b18.1: Within its year: [its daughters] were born in one of its years; and the daughters and their young can be found in one year, so that the daughters are tithed, only in a leap year; for example, it gave birth at the beginning of a year and its daughters at the end of their year.
gershom:b19.1: And let her give birth again: the kid, and give birth together with them, and there will be ten between the daughters and the mothers.
